ask: Which of the following does a security control category describe?

options.why: A category sorts a control by how it is carried out: by a system, by policy, by people or by a physical barrier.
The goal (stop, discourage, detect and so on) is the control type, a separate label from the category.
Budget and ownership play no part in sorting controls into categories.

options.t: When the control was last tested
options.why: Test dates matter for audits, but categories sort controls by how they are implemented.

explain: Technical, managerial, operational and physical describe how a control is carried out. What the control is meant to achieve is its type, a second label.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

ask: Which of the following lists the four security control categories?

options.why: Financial is not a control category, and physical, for controls that protect spaces and equipment, is missing.
Logical is another name for technical, so this list repeats one category and leaves out managerial.
These four cover controls enforced by systems, set by policy, done by people and built into the physical space.
Hardware, software and firmware are what a technical control is built from, not separate categories.

explain: The categories are technical (a system enforces it), managerial (policies and risk decisions), operational (people carry it out) and physical (protects spaces and assets).

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A hospital's administration approves a written rule that every visitor must wear a visitor badge at all times while inside the building.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the approved rule belong to?

options.why: No system enforces anything here; the control is a decision written down.
An approved rule is a policy decision, which is the managerial category.
The badge is a tangible item, but the control asked about is the approved rule, which is a document.
Staff checking badges would be operational, but the rule itself is a governing document.

detail: approves a written rule
explain: Policies and risk decisions are managerial controls. The rule sets what must happen; other controls carry it out.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A city water utility assigns two staff members to watch the plant's network alerts around the clock and phone the engineer on duty when one looks real.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes this arrangement?

options.why: The alerts come from systems, but the arrangement is people judging them, not a system enforcing a rule.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is routine work done by staff.
Nothing here protects a building, room or piece of equipment.
People watching alerts and deciding when to call is security work carried out by people day to day.

detail: assigns two staff members to watch
explain: Operational controls are carried out by people as part of daily operations. Here staff do the watching and the judging.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A bus depot surrounds its overnight parking yard with a tall fence that has a single gate.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the fence belong to?

options.why: No hardware, software or firmware enforces a rule here; the fence is a barrier.
No person performs a task; the fence works simply by being there.
A fence is not a policy or a risk decision.
A fence protects a tangible space, which is the physical category.

detail: a tall fence that has a single gate
explain: Physical controls protect tangible spaces and assets. A fence around a yard is the plainest example.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A retailer's security standard states that every laptop must use disk encryption. The IT team then turns on the built-in encryption feature on each laptop.
ask: Which of the following gives the categories of the standard and of the encryption feature, in that order?

options.why: This reverses them: the standard is the managerial control and the feature is the technical one.
The standard is a governing document (managerial); the encryption is enforced by the laptop itself (technical).
The standard is a governing document, not a routine task people perform.
Disk encryption is enforced by software on the laptop, not by a barrier around a space.

detail: The IT team then turns on the built-in encryption feature
explain: A rule that requires encryption and the encryption itself are two controls in two categories. The standard is managerial and the running encryption is technical.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: Password resets at a telecom provider used to need a help desk agent to confirm each caller. Now a self-service portal checks a one-time code and resets the password with no agent involved.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the identity check now?

options.why: The portal checks the code by itself with no person deciding, so a system enforces it.
It was operational while an agent confirmed callers, but no person performs the check any more.
No policy or risk decision is described; the change is in who performs the check.
Nothing here protects a space or a piece of equipment.

detail: with no agent involved
explain: Operational means people do it; technical means a system does it. Once the portal decides each reset, the check is technical.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: An auditor sorting a bakery chain's controls places 'antivirus on every till' under the people category because cashiers use the tills all day.
ask: Which of the following control categories should the auditor have used?

options.why: Cashiers use the tills, but they do not carry out the antivirus control; the software does.
The tills are equipment, but antivirus protects them through software, not a barrier.
Antivirus software works by itself on each till, with no person deciding each case.
Antivirus is not a policy or a risk decision.

detail: because cashiers use the tills all day
explain: The category follows who or what carries out the control, not who uses the protected equipment. Antivirus is enforced by software, so it is technical.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A security administrator at an electric cooperative exports the control register below.
ask: Which of the following control categories applies to CTRL-07?

lines: CTRL-07  Acceptable use document signed by each new hire
CTRL-12  Badge reader on the data hall door
CTRL-19  Endpoint agent blocks unsigned programs
CTRL-23  Help desk calls the user back before a reset

options.why: That fits CTRL-19, where the endpoint agent enforces the rule; CTRL-07 is a document.
An acceptable use document is a policy that guides behavior, which is managerial.
That fits CTRL-12, the badge reader on a door; CTRL-07 protects no space.
That fits CTRL-23, a task the help desk performs; CTRL-07 is a policy.

detail: Acceptable use document signed by each new hire
explain: Policies such as an acceptable use document are managerial controls. The other lines show one control from each of the other three categories.

ask: Which of the following statements about control categories are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: Operational means people carry the control out
options.why: Operational controls are performed by people in daily work.

options.t: Physical means a system enforces the rule
options.why: A system enforcing a rule is technical; physical controls protect spaces and assets.
Administrative is the other name for the managerial category.
Written policies are managerial; technical controls are enforced by hardware, software or firmware.

options.t: A category names the goal a control serves
options.why: The goal is the control type; the category is how the control is implemented.

explain: Operational controls are carried out by people, and managerial is also called administrative. A category says how a control is implemented, never what goal it serves.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

ask: Which of the following describes a technical control?

options.why: Technical controls run in hardware, software or firmware, so the system applies them rather than a person.

options.t: Staff carry it out as daily work
options.why: That describes an operational control, which people perform.

options.t: Leadership sets it in a written policy
options.why: That describes a managerial control, made of policies and risk decisions.

options.t: A barrier guards a room or building
options.why: That describes a physical control, which protects tangible spaces.

explain: A technical control is implemented with technology, so the system enforces it rather than a person. Firewalls and antivirus are classic examples.

ask: Which of the following is another name for the technical control category?

options.why: Administrative is the other name for managerial, not technical.
Operational is its own category, for controls people carry out.
Physical is its own category, for controls that protect spaces and assets.
Logical control is an older name for a technical control.

explain: Technical controls are also called logical controls. Administrative is the other name for managerial controls.

stem: A law firm's file server lets only members of the litigation group open the case folders. Requests from anyone else are refused by the operating system.
ask: Which of the following control categories does this describe?

options.why: No document or risk decision does the work; the server refuses the requests itself.
No person checks each request.
Operating system permissions are enforced by the system on every request.
Nothing guards a room or device; the protection is on the folders.

detail: refused by the operating system
explain: Operating system permissions are a standard technical control: the system decides every request with no person involved.

stem: Two controls protect the payroll database at a freight company. An analyst reads the database's access report every Friday, and the database encrypts every record it stores.
ask: Which of the following control categories fits the record encryption?

options.why: That fits the Friday report reading, which a person performs; the encryption needs no person.
No policy or risk decision is described for the encryption.
The database applies the encryption itself, so a system enforces it.
Encryption protects data, not a room or piece of equipment.

detail: the database encrypts every record it stores
explain: Encryption applied by the system is technical. The analyst reading reports is the contrast: a person performing a task is operational.

stem: A school district's laptops run antivirus software that quarantines a harmful download the moment it arrives, before any staff member looks at it.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the antivirus software belong to?

options.why: No staff member is involved; the software acts on its own.
The software is not a policy or a risk decision.
It protects files on the laptop, not a space or the laptop as an object.
The software acts by itself the moment the file arrives, which is a system enforcing a rule.

detail: before any staff member looks at it
explain: Antivirus software is one of the classic technical controls: it enforces its rules without a person deciding each case.

stem: A network engineer at a hotel group writes a rule that blocks remote desktop connections from outside. The edge firewall now applies it to every incoming connection.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the firewall applying the rule?

options.why: Deciding what the rule should be can be managerial, but the stem asks about the firewall applying it.
Once written, the rule is applied by the firewall to every connection with no person deciding.
Writing the rule is a one-time act by a person; applying it is done by the firewall.
The rule filters network traffic; nothing guards a room or device.

detail: The edge firewall now applies it to every incoming connection
explain: Someone writes a technical rule once, then the system applies it every time. The applying is the technical control.

stem: A vendor questionnaire from a health insurer asks a supplier to list its logical controls that protect member data.
ask: Which of the following controls belongs under that heading?

options.why: Logical is another name for technical, and permissions are enforced by the system.
A policy is managerial, also called administrative, not logical.
Locked cabinets protect tangible items, which is physical.
A review that people carry out is operational.

detail: list its logical controls
explain: Logical controls are technical controls. File permissions are enforced by the system, so they belong on the list.

stem: The badge server at a research lab rejects any badge that the HR system has marked as revoked, even when the badge itself is undamaged and still in date.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the badge server's rejection?

options.why: The server applies the revocation rule by itself to every badge, so a system enforces it.
The reader on the door is physical, but the stem asks about the server rule that rejects revoked badges.
No person checks each badge; the server decides.
Revoking a badge may follow a policy, but the rejection itself is done by the server.

detail: rejects any badge that the HR system has marked as revoked
edge: A badge reader that controls entry to a space is physical, but the rule run by the badge server is enforced by a system, which is technical.
explain: A badge system has parts in two categories: the reader on the door is physical, and the server rule that rejects revoked badges is technical.

stem: A network administrator at a county library reviews two lines that the edge firewall applies to all traffic.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes these lines?

lines: rule 10  permit tcp any host 198.51.100.20 eq 443
rule 20  deny   ip  any host 198.51.100.20

options.why: The lines are enforced by a device; they are not a policy document or a risk decision.
No person checks each connection.
The firewall enforces the lines on every packet with no person deciding.
The lines filter network traffic; nothing guards a room or device.

detail: the edge firewall applies to all traffic
explain: Firewall rules are a classic technical control. A person wrote them once, but the firewall applies them to every connection.

stem: The security lead at a physiotherapy practice must list two technical controls for an upcoming audit.
ask: Which of the following belong on the list? (Select TWO)

options.t: A visitor sign-in sheet at reception
options.why: People fill in and check a sign-in sheet; no system enforces it.
Encryption is applied by the laptop itself, so a system enforces it.
A risk assessment is a managerial control.
The system locks the account by itself after the failed attempts.
Locks protect a space, which is a physical control.

detail: must list two technical controls
explain: Disk encryption and account lockout are both enforced by systems. A sign-in sheet is people work, a risk assessment is managerial and a lock is physical.

ask: Which of the following describes a managerial control?

options.t: A system enforcing a rule by itself
options.why: That describes a technical control.
Managerial controls design and oversee security through policies, standards and risk assessments.
That describes an operational control.

options.t: A lock or fence guarding a space
options.why: That describes a physical control.

explain: Managerial controls are documents and decisions, not technology. They guide how the organization manages security.

ask: Which of the following control categories is also called administrative?

options.why: The other name for technical is logical.
Operational controls are carried out by people; they have no administrative alias.
Physical controls protect spaces and assets; they are not called administrative.
Administrative is the other name for managerial controls.

explain: Managerial controls are also called administrative controls. Technical controls are also called logical controls.

stem: Leadership at a seed company approves an offboarding policy. It says every departing employee's accounts must be closed on their last day.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the approved policy belong to?

options.why: The accounts may be closed in a system later, but the policy itself is a document, not technology.
Staff closing the accounts would be operational; the policy sets the rule they follow.
A policy protects no room or piece of equipment.
An offboarding policy approved by leadership is a managerial control.

detail: Leadership at a seed company approves an offboarding policy
explain: Onboarding and offboarding policies approved by leadership are managerial controls. The work of closing accounts is a separate control.

stem: A card payment processor hires an outside firm to rate the likelihood and impact of each threat to its payment systems. The results go to the board.
ask: Which of the following control categories fits this exercise?

options.why: The firm rates risks for leadership; this is oversight, not routine security work done by staff.
A risk assessment that informs leadership is a managerial control.
No system enforces anything; the output is a set of ratings.
Nothing protects a space or a piece of equipment.

detail: rate the likelihood and impact of each threat
explain: Risk assessments are a typical managerial control. They shape what the organization decides to do about security.

stem: At a museum, a junior analyst keeps the risk register up to date, recording each risk, its owner and the decision taken about it.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the risk register fall under?

options.why: The register records risk ownership and decisions, which is managerial whoever maintains it.
An analyst updates it, but the register records risk decisions and oversight, which is managerial.
The register enforces nothing; it is a record of decisions.
It protects no space or equipment.

detail: recording each risk, its owner and the decision taken about it
explain: Managerial does not mean done by managers. A risk register is a managerial control even when an analyst keeps it.

stem: The board of a regional bank decides that every employee must complete security awareness training each year and approves funding for the program.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the board's decision?

options.why: Delivering the training to staff is operational, but the stem asks about the decision to require it.
No system enforces anything here.
Requiring training and funding a program is a governance decision, which is managerial.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.

detail: decides that every employee must complete security awareness training
edge: Training sessions delivered to staff are operational, but the stem describes the board deciding to require training, which is managerial.
explain: The decision to require training is managerial; running the sessions is operational. The stem is about the board deciding.

stem: A logistics firm adds a clause to all of its supplier contracts. The clause requires each supplier to meet a list of security requirements and to report any data breach within 48 hours.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the contract clause belong to?

options.why: No routine task is being performed; the clause sets requirements.
A vendor security requirement set in a contract is a governance decision, which is managerial.
A contract clause is not enforced by any system.
A contract protects no space or equipment.

detail: requires each supplier to meet a list of security requirements
explain: Requirements set for vendors are managerial controls: they direct what others must do rather than blocking anything themselves.

stem: A security analyst at a cosmetics maker receives the message below from the security office.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the message announce?

lines: From: security-office@cosmetics.example
Subject: New standard for customer data
From 1 March, customer files may be stored only in the approved document vault.

options.why: The message sets a new standard for how data is stored, which is managerial.
The vault may enforce access later, but the message sets a standard; it enforces nothing itself.
No routine task performed by people is described; a standard is set.
The standard protects files, not a room or piece of equipment.

detail: customer files may be stored only in the approved document vault
explain: Standards and policies are managerial controls. The message sets a rule that other controls will carry out.

stem: Each year, the leadership team at a shipping firm compares the results of its security program with the goals it set and decides what to fund next.
ask: Which of the following control categories does this yearly review fall under?

options.why: This is not routine security work on systems; it is leadership overseeing the program.
No system enforces anything; leadership is making decisions.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.
Reviewing results against goals and deciding what to fund is oversight of security, which is managerial.

detail: compares the results of its security program with the goals it set
explain: Managerial controls include management reviewing results and adjusting the program. Deciding what to fund is a governance decision.

stem: A hospital's governance committee asks the security team for a list of its managerial controls.
ask: Which of the following belong on the list? (Select TWO)

options.why: Guards are people doing security work on site, not a policy or risk decision.
Antivirus is enforced by software, which is technical.
A standard that guides how data is handled is managerial.

options.t: Weekly log review by an analyst
options.why: A person reviewing logs is operational work.
A risk assessment is a typical managerial control.

detail: a list of its managerial controls
explain: Standards and risk assessments are documents and decisions, so they are managerial. Guards, antivirus and log reviews fall in other categories.

ask: Which of the following describes an operational control?

options.t: A system enforces it with no person
options.why: That describes a technical control.

options.t: Leadership decides it in a policy
options.why: That describes a managerial control.

options.t: People perform it in daily work
options.why: Operational controls are carried out by people as part of daily operations.

options.t: A barrier protects a room or site
options.why: That describes a physical control.

explain: Operational controls are implemented by people rather than by systems. Managerial sets the policy; operational is people doing the work.

ask: Which of the following controls is operational?

options.why: Antivirus is software enforcing rules by itself, which is technical.
A written policy is managerial.
Training is delivered and followed by people, which makes it operational.

options.t: Locks on the server room doors
options.why: Locks protect a space, which is physical.

explain: Security awareness training is the classic operational control: people carry it out as part of their work.

stem: At a call center, a supervisor walks the floor at the end of each shift and checks that no customer printouts are left on desks.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the supervisor's check?

options.why: Nothing tangible blocks access here; a person performs the check.
A rule about printouts would be managerial, but the walk is the work itself.
No system enforces the check.
A person performing a routine check during daily operations is operational.

detail: a supervisor walks the floor at the end of each shift
explain: Operational controls are tasks people carry out in daily work. A supervisor checking desks each shift is one.

stem: At a pharmaceutical warehouse, guards at the front desk compare each visitor's photo ID with the expected visitor list before letting anyone in.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the guards' checks?

options.why: A guard can count as physical when the focus is the barrier, but here the focus is the person checking IDs.
Guards checking IDs is people doing security work, which the stem stresses.
No system makes the decision; the guards compare IDs themselves.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is a task performed at the desk.

detail: compare each visitor's photo ID with the expected visitor list
edge: A guard can be counted as physical when the focus is the barrier, but this stem focuses on the person doing the checking, which is operational.
explain: Security guards checking IDs is a standard operational example. The category follows what the stem stresses: here, the work the guards do.

stem: Each morning, an analyst at an online retailer reads the previous night's login records and flags anything unusual to her manager.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the morning review belong to?

options.why: A person reviewing records as part of daily work is operational.
The records come from systems, but a person reads and judges them.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is routine work.
Nothing protects a space or a device.

detail: an analyst at an online retailer reads the previous night's login records
explain: Staff performing regular log reviews is an operational control. The logs are produced by systems, but the review is people doing the work.

stem: When an employee at a staffing agency asks for access to the finance share, an administrator phones the employee's manager to confirm the request before granting it.
ask: Which of the following explains why the phone confirmation is an operational control?

options.t: A person performs the check by hand
options.why: The administrator makes the call as part of daily work, which is what makes it operational.
No system decides anything; the administrator chooses to call and judges the answer.

options.t: A written rule makes the check happen
options.why: A rule requiring confirmation would be managerial, but the stem describes the call itself.
The call protects access to a file share, not a room or building.

detail: an administrator phones the employee's manager to confirm
explain: A verification step that a person performs in daily work is operational. If a system required and checked the approval, it would be technical.

stem: A trainer at a city council runs hands-on sessions in which staff practice spotting and reporting suspicious emails.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the sessions?

options.why: Deciding to require training is managerial, but the stem describes sessions being delivered.
No system enforces anything; a trainer and staff do the work.
Delivering training to staff is security work people carry out, which is operational.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.

detail: runs hands-on sessions
edge: The decision to require training is managerial, but the stem describes the sessions themselves being run, which is operational.
explain: Awareness training delivered to staff is the classic operational control. The decision behind it would be managerial.

stem: Every quarter, department heads at an insurance broker go through the list of staff who can open client folders and confirm that each one still needs access.
ask: Which of the following explains why this access review is an operational control?

options.t: Managers are the ones carrying it out
options.why: Being done by managers does not make it managerial; managerial does not mean done by managers.

options.t: People perform it as routine work
options.why: A user access review is a routine task people carry out, which is operational.

options.t: It records how the firm decides on risk
options.why: The review confirms access; it does not record risk decisions, which would be managerial.

options.t: A system decides who keeps their rights
options.why: People confirm each entry; no system makes the decision.

detail: go through the list of staff who can open client folders
explain: User access reviews are operational controls: people carry them out on a schedule. Who performs them does not make them managerial.

stem: A system administrator at a seaport keeps the shift checklist below.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the 07:00 entry?

lines: 06:00  Night shift handover signed
06:15  Server room door checked and found locked
07:00  Admin group members compared with the approved list, 0 differences

options.why: No system rule is recorded; the checklist records a person doing the comparison.
The 06:15 entry concerns a door; the 07:00 entry is about group membership.
No policy or risk decision is recorded; it is a routine check.
The entry records a person comparing group members by hand as part of the shift.

detail: Admin group members compared with the approved list
explain: A routine check that a person performs and records is operational. The checklist shows the work being done by staff.

stem: The manager of a distribution center must add two controls in the operational category before the next audit.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.t: Guards checking driver IDs at the gate
options.why: Guards checking IDs is work people do, which is operational.

options.t: A badge reader on the warehouse door
options.why: A badge reader on a door is a physical control.

options.t: An acceptable use policy for handheld scanners
options.why: A policy is a managerial control.

options.t: Supervisors reviewing camera footage each shift
options.why: People reviewing footage on a schedule is operational work.
The system locks the account by itself, which is technical.

detail: two controls in the operational category
explain: Operational controls are carried out by people: guards checking IDs and supervisors reviewing footage. The others are physical, managerial and technical.

ask: Which of the following describes a physical control?

options.t: A system enforces it in software
options.why: That describes a technical control.

options.t: People perform it as routine work
options.why: That describes an operational control.

options.t: Leadership approves it as a policy
options.why: That describes a managerial control.

options.t: It protects buildings, rooms or equipment
options.why: Physical controls limit access to tangible spaces and assets.

explain: A physical control limits physical access to buildings, rooms or equipment, or protects tangible assets. Fences and door locks are examples.

ask: Which of the following controls belongs to the physical category?

options.why: Firewall rules are enforced by a system, which is technical.
Bollards are posts that protect a building or space, a physical control.
Staff reviewing logs is operational work.
A risk assessment is a managerial control.

explain: Bollards, fences, locks and badge systems are physical controls. They protect the physical environment.

stem: A stadium installs a row of steel posts in front of its ticket office so that no vehicle can reach the windows.
ask: Which of the following control categories do the steel posts belong to?

options.why: The posts are a tangible barrier protecting a building.
The posts enforce nothing through software or firmware; they are a barrier.
No person performs a task; the posts work by being there.
The posts are not a policy or a risk decision.

detail: a row of steel posts in front of its ticket office
explain: Posts that keep vehicles away from a building are bollards, a physical control.

stem: A data center fits a lock to every server rack and gives the keys to only two engineers.
ask: Which of the following control categories do the rack locks belong to?

options.why: Deciding who holds keys is a managerial choice, but the locks themselves protect the equipment.
No routine task is described; the locks work by being there.
Rack locks limit physical access to equipment.
A key lock involves no software or firmware enforcing a rule.

detail: fits a lock to every server rack
explain: Locks on racks protect tangible equipment, so they are physical controls.

stem: A research lab installs readers that unlock the lab door only when an approved badge is tapped.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the readers on the door?

options.why: The badge system's software rules can count as technical, but the readers on the door control entry to a room.
The readers control entry to a space, which makes them physical even though they contain electronics.
No person checks each badge at the door.
The readers are not a policy or risk decision.

detail: readers that unlock the lab door
edge: The badge system's database rules can be described as technical, but a reader on a door controls entry to a space, so it is physical.
explain: Access badges and readers are physical controls because they control entry to a space. Only the rules in the badge database lean technical.

stem: A car plant builds a booth at its only vehicle gate, with a barrier arm that stays down until a vehicle is cleared.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the booth and barrier arm?

options.why: A booth and a barrier arm are tangible structures controlling entry to the site.
The person working in the booth does operational work, but the stem asks about the booth and arm.
No software rule is described; the arm is a barrier.
Neither is a policy or a risk decision.

detail: a barrier arm that stays down until a vehicle is cleared
edge: Whoever staffs the booth does operational work, but the booth and the barrier arm are tangible structures, which are physical.
explain: Guard shacks and barriers are physical controls. The person on duty would be the operational part.

stem: A broadcaster installs a gas fire suppression system and a backup generator in the room that holds its transmission servers.
ask: Which of the following control categories do these protections belong to?

options.why: They do not enforce access or data rules through software; they protect the room and its power.
No routine task performed by people is described.
Neither is a policy or a risk decision.
Fire suppression and backup power protect the physical environment of the servers.

detail: a gas fire suppression system and a backup generator
explain: Physical controls also protect the supporting environment, such as fire suppression and backup power, which keeps equipment available.

stem: A cattle feed company puts a three-meter fence topped with wire around its yard so that intruders cannot climb in.
ask: Which of the following classifies the fence correctly?

options.why: The labels are swapped: physical is a category and preventive is a type.
No person performs a task; the fence is a tangible barrier, so the category is physical.
A fence is physical by category, and stopping intruders climbing in is preventive.
Corrective acts after an event to repair damage; the fence stops intruders beforehand.

detail: so that intruders cannot climb in
explain: Physical is a category, not a type. A fence that stops intruders is physical in category and preventive in type.

stem: A parking garage fits bright lights on every level and in every stairwell so that the whole building stays well lit at night.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the lighting belong to?

options.why: No software or firmware enforces a rule here.
No person performs a routine task; the lights work by being on.
Lighting protects a tangible space, which is a physical control.
Lighting is not a policy or risk decision.

detail: fits bright lights on every level and in every stairwell
explain: Security lighting is a physical control: it protects the physical environment of a site.

stem: A clinic must add two physical controls to protect the room where it keeps medicines.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.t: A policy limiting who may enter
options.why: A policy is a managerial control.

options.t: A locked door with a badge reader
options.why: A lock and badge reader control entry to the room, which is physical.

options.t: Weekly stock counts by a pharmacist
options.why: A person counting stock is operational work.

options.t: Alerts when the stock database changes
options.why: Alerts generated by a system are technical.

options.t: A camera covering the room entrance
options.why: A camera watching a space is a physical control.

detail: add two physical controls
explain: Physical controls include locks, badge readers and cameras covering a space. A policy, a stock count and system alerts belong to other categories.

ask: Which of the following does a security control type describe?

options.why: How a control is implemented is its category, a separate label.
The supplier plays no part in a control type.
Location does not decide the type; the goal does.
A type names the job a control does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, compensate or direct.

explain: Control types name the goal a control serves. The category (technical, managerial, operational, physical) is a separate question about how it is implemented.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

ask: Which of the following lists only control types?

options.why: Technical and physical are categories, not types.
All three are control types: stop it, identify it, fix it after.
These are all categories, which describe how a control is implemented.
Physical is a category, not a type.

explain: The six types are preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating and directive. Technical, managerial, operational and physical are categories.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A hotel posts a guard at its service entrance. The guard turns away anyone without a staff badge and writes down the name of every person who passes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the guard serve? (Select TWO)

options.why: Turning away people without a badge stops them entering.
Nothing has gone wrong that needs repair.
The guard is not standing in for a control that cannot be used.
The guard enforces entry rather than only telling people what to do.
Writing down every person who passes records events for later investigation.

detail: turns away anyone without a staff badge and writes down the name of every person
explain: One control can serve several types. Turning people away is preventive and recording who passes is detective.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: An auditor at a shipping line asks what goal the new alarm on the loading dock door serves. The alarm sounds and logs an entry when the door opens after hours, but it does not lock anything.
ask: Which of the following answers the auditor's question?

options.why: The alarm identifies and records the door opening, which is the detective goal.
Physical is a category, how the control is implemented; the auditor asked what goal it serves.
The alarm does not lock anything, so it blocks nothing.
Technical is a category, not a goal; the auditor asked for the type.

detail: it does not lock anything
explain: The question asks for a type, so category answers are out. An alarm that records the opening but blocks nothing is detective.

source.chapter: Classifying one control by category and type (worked method)

stem: A storage company puts up signs along its fence warning that the yard is monitored and intruders will be prosecuted. The signs do not stop anyone from climbing over.
ask: Which of the following control types do the signs serve?

options.why: The signs try to discourage intruders without stopping them.
The signs do not stop anyone climbing over, and preventive controls actually block.
The signs record nothing and raise no alert.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

detail: The signs do not stop anyone from climbing over
explain: Deterrent controls discourage but do not stop. Preventive controls actually block the act.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A design review of a bank's mobile app finds strong controls that block attacks, but nothing that would reveal when an attack gets through.
ask: Which of the following control types is missing?

options.why: The review says the blocking controls are already strong.
Discouraging attackers would not reveal an attack that got through.
Detective controls identify and record events, which is what the review found missing.
Telling people what to do would not reveal an attack that got through.

detail: nothing that would reveal when an attack gets through
explain: A design with only preventive controls has no way to know when they fail. Detective controls fill that gap.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A parking operator mounts large, obvious cameras at each entrance with a sign naming them. The stated reason is to make car thieves choose another lot.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the stated reason for the cameras?

options.why: The cameras also record, which is detective, but the stated reason is to make thieves go elsewhere.
Making thieves choose another lot is discouraging the attempt, which is deterrence.
Cameras do not physically stop anyone entering.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

detail: The stated reason is to make car thieves choose another lot
edge: A visible camera is both detective and deterrent, and the stem names its purpose as making thieves choose another lot, which is the deterrent job.
explain: One control can serve several types; the answer follows what the stem stresses. Here the stated reason is to discourage, so deterrent fits best.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A software firm's handbook says developers must not paste customer data into chat tools. Nothing in the chat tools blocks it.
ask: Which of the following control types does the handbook rule provide?

options.why: Nothing in the tools blocks the pasting, so nothing is prevented.
The rule records nothing and raises no alert.
The rule is not standing in for a control that cannot be used.
The rule tells people what not to do and relies on them to comply.

detail: Nothing in the chat tools blocks it
explain: A directive control instructs people and relies on compliance. With nothing blocking the act, the rule is directive, not preventive.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A ferry operator plans three controls for its engine room: a warning sign on the door, a lock on the door, and a sensor that alerts the bridge when the door opens.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sensor provide?

options.why: That is the warning sign's job; the sensor reports what happens.
That is the lock's job; the sensor blocks nothing.
The sensor repairs nothing after an event.
The sensor identifies the door opening and alerts, which is detective.

detail: a sensor that alerts the bridge when the door opens
explain: A sound design covers several stages: the sign discourages, the lock blocks, and the sensor detects.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

ask: Which of the following statements about control types are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: Preventive acts only after an incident
options.why: Preventive acts before an incident; corrective acts after.

options.t: One control can serve several types
options.why: A guard, for example, can prevent, deter and detect at once.

options.t: Deterrent discourages but does not stop
options.why: Deterrent works on the attacker's choice; preventive actually blocks.
Directive only instructs people and relies on them to comply.

options.t: Compensating repairs damage after an attack
options.why: Repairing after an attack is corrective; compensating substitutes for a missing control.

explain: One control can have several types, and deterrent controls discourage without stopping. The other statements mix up preventive, directive, corrective and compensating.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

ask: Which of the following describes a preventive control?

options.t: It discourages an attempt without stopping it
options.why: That describes a deterrent control.

options.t: It blocks an incident before it happens
options.why: Preventive controls stop the event before it occurs by restricting access or actions.

options.t: It records an event so it can be investigated
options.why: That describes a detective control.

options.t: It restores systems after an event
options.why: That describes a corrective control.

explain: A preventive control blocks an incident from happening in the first place. Deterrent only discourages; preventive actually blocks.

ask: Which of the following controls is preventive?

options.why: Locking the account blocks further guessing.

options.t: A banner warning that misuse is prosecuted
options.why: A warning banner discourages but does not block, which is deterrent.
Log review identifies events after they happen, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

explain: Account lockout policies, door locks and firewall rules that block traffic are standard preventive controls.

stem: A bakery chain fits its stockroom with a door that stays locked until an employee enters the right code, so no one else can walk in.
ask: Which of the following control types does the coded lock provide?

options.why: The lock does not rely on anyone choosing to stay out; it keeps them out.
The lock does not record or alert; it blocks.
The lock blocks entry for anyone without the code.
Nothing has happened yet that needs repair.

detail: so no one else can walk in
explain: A door lock is a standard preventive control: it stops the act before it happens.

stem: A dental practice's firewall drops every inbound connection from the internet to its patient database server before the connection reaches the server.
ask: Which of the following control types does the firewall provide here?

options.why: Dropping the connection stops it rather than only reporting it.
Dropping the connection before it arrives blocks it.
Nothing depends on the sender choosing to stop; the connection is refused.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

detail: before the connection reaches the server
explain: A firewall rule blocking inbound traffic is a classic preventive control.

stem: A university's network team places a sensor in line with campus traffic. The sensor drops any packet that matches a known attack pattern.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sensor?

options.why: The sensor drops the matching packets, which blocks the attack.
The sensor does identify attack patterns, but it also drops the packets, which goes past detection.
Nothing here relies on discouraging the attacker.
The sensor acts before the packet arrives, not after damage.

detail: drops any packet that matches a known attack pattern
edge: Identifying an attack is detective, but this sensor also drops the packets: an IPS (intrusion prevention system) is preventive, while an IDS that only alerts is detective.
explain: An IDS (intrusion detection system) only alerts and is detective. An IPS drops traffic and is preventive, and this sensor drops packets.

stem: A clinic installs the vendor fix for a flaw in its scheduling software on the day the fix is released, before anyone has tried to exploit the flaw.
ask: Which of the following control types does installing the fix provide here?

options.why: Patching is corrective when it fixes a system already exploited; here nothing has happened yet.
The fix identifies nothing; it removes the flaw.
The fix is the required control itself, not a substitute for one.
Fixing the flaw before any attack stops the attack from being possible.

detail: before anyone has tried to exploit the flaw
explain: Patching is preventive when done before exploitation and corrective when done to fix an exploited system. The timing in the stem decides.

stem: A law office turns on full-disk encryption on its laptops so that the files on a stolen laptop cannot be read.
ask: Which of the following control types does the encryption provide?

options.why: Encryption does not record or report a theft.
Encryption is in place before any theft; corrective acts after.
Encryption prevents unauthorized reading of the files.
Encryption does not depend on discouraging a thief; it keeps the files unreadable.

detail: cannot be read
explain: Encryption is counted as preventive because it prevents disclosure of stolen data, even though the laptop itself can still be taken.

stem: A payroll firm configures its workstations so that only programs on an approved list can start. Any other program is refused.
ask: Which of the following control types does this configuration provide?

options.why: A list of approved programs in a handbook would be directive; here the workstation refuses the rest.
The configuration blocks programs rather than only reporting them.
Programs not on the list are refused, so they never run.
Nothing here substitutes for a control that cannot be used.

detail: Any other program is refused
explain: An application allow list is preventive: unapproved programs are blocked before they run.

stem: An administrator at a seafood exporter applies the rules below to the mail server's network interface.
ask: Which of the following control types does the second rule provide?

lines: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 192.0.2.25 eq 25
access-list 110 deny ip any host 192.0.2.25

options.why: The rule does not alert; it refuses the traffic.
No one is shown a warning; the traffic is simply blocked.
Nothing has gone wrong that needs repair.
The rule refuses all other traffic to the server before it arrives.

detail: access-list 110 deny ip any host 192.0.2.25
explain: A deny rule blocks traffic before it reaches the server, which is preventive. The first rule lets mail through and the second blocks everything else.

stem: A warehouse manager wants controls that actually stop an intruder getting in, rather than ones that only discourage or record an attempt.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.t: A No Entry sign on the fence
options.why: A sign only instructs or discourages; it stops no one.
A camera records the attempt; it does not stop it.
Lighting discourages but does not block entry.

options.t: A locked gate at the loading bay
options.why: A locked gate blocks entry.

options.t: An access control vestibule at the entrance
options.why: A vestibule holds a person until they are cleared, which blocks entry.

detail: actually stop an intruder getting in
explain: Preventive controls block the act: locked gates and access control vestibules do. Signs and lighting only discourage, and cameras only record.

ask: Which of the following describes a deterrent control?

options.t: It blocks an attempt before it starts
options.why: That describes a preventive control.

options.t: It discourages but does not stop
options.why: A deterrent works on the attacker's choice and does not block the attempt.

options.t: It identifies an event and raises an alert
options.why: That describes a detective control.

options.t: It repairs systems after an incident
options.why: That describes a corrective control.

explain: A deterrent control discourages someone from trying without physically or technically stopping them. A determined attacker can ignore it.

ask: Which of the following controls is a deterrent?

options.t: A login banner warning of prosecution
options.why: A warning of prosecution discourages misuse but does not block a login.

options.t: A firewall rule blocking inbound traffic
options.why: Blocking traffic is preventive.
An alert identifies an event, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

explain: Login banners, visible guards and warnings of consequences are deterrent controls: they discourage without stopping.

stem: A software company shows a notice on every staff login screen saying that misuse can lead to dismissal. Staff can still sign in and use the system as normal.
ask: Which of the following control types does the notice serve?

options.why: The notice warns of a consequence to discourage misuse without blocking anyone.
The notice blocks nothing; staff still sign in as normal.
The notice itself records nothing and raises no alert.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

detail: Staff can still sign in and use the system as normal
explain: A warning that discourages misuse but stops nothing is deterrent. A preventive control would actually block the action.

stem: An architecture firm places a uniformed guard at its reception desk. The firm says the main reason is so that people with bad intentions decide not to try entering.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the stated reason for the guard?

options.why: A guard can also block entry, but the stated reason is to make people decide not to try.
The stated reason says nothing about identifying or recording events.
Making people decide not to try is discouraging the attempt, which is deterrence.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

detail: so that people with bad intentions decide not to try entering
edge: A guard can serve as preventive too, but the stem names the reason as making people decide not to try, which is the deterrent job.
explain: A visible guard at reception is a standard deterrent example. One control can serve several types, so follow the reason the stem gives.

stem: A trading firm's handbook states that sharing a trading password will lead to demotion. Nothing in the trading systems stops a trader from sharing one.
ask: Which of the following control types does the threat of demotion serve?

options.why: Nothing stops a trader from sharing, so nothing is prevented.
The threat of demotion discourages sharing without stopping it.
The threat does not identify or record any sharing.
Nothing is repaired; the threat acts before any sharing.

detail: will lead to demotion
explain: A threat of demotion for policy violations is a deterrent control: it has a psychological effect only, and it blocks nothing.

stem: The door of a data center carries a sign that reads: 'Unauthorized entry will be reported to the police.'
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sign?

options.why: A sign telling people what to do would be directive, but this one warns of what happens.
The sign does not stop anyone opening the door.
The sign records nothing and raises no alert.
The sign warns of a consequence, which discourages entry.

detail: will be reported to the police
edge: A directive sign instructs people (such as 'Authorized staff only'); this sign warns of a consequence, which makes it deterrent.
explain: Directive instructs; deterrent warns of consequences. A sign that names a consequence for entering is deterrent.

stem: A car dealership floods its lot with bright lights at night so that thieves can see they would easily be noticed and move on.
ask: Which of the following control types does the lighting serve?

options.why: The lights record nothing and raise no alert.
A thief can still walk onto the lot; nothing blocks them.
The lights are not standing in for a control that cannot be used.
The lighting aims to make thieves move on, which discourages the attempt.

detail: so that thieves can see they would easily be noticed and move on
explain: Bright lighting is a deterrent control: it raises the perceived risk of being seen without physically stopping anyone.

stem: A health clinic protects its remote admin portal only with a warning banner. An attacker who ignores the warning signs in with a stolen password.
ask: Which of the following control types would have stopped the sign-in?

options.why: The banner is already deterrent, and the attacker ignored it.
A preventive control blocks the action, which a warning cannot do.
Detection could notice the sign-in afterward but would not stop it.
Instructions rely on compliance, which this attacker ignores.

detail: An attacker who ignores the warning
explain: A deterrent has a psychological effect only, so a determined attacker can ignore it. Only a preventive control actually blocks the sign-in.

stem: Every remote session to a county records server begins with the screen below.
ask: Which of the following control types does this screen provide?

lines: NOTICE: All sessions on this server are logged.
Misuse will be referred for prosecution.
Press Enter to continue.

options.why: The screen warns of prosecution to discourage misuse.
Pressing Enter lets anyone continue, so nothing is blocked.
The logging behind the screen is detective, but the screen itself only warns.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

detail: Misuse will be referred for prosecution.
explain: A login banner warning that misuse will be prosecuted is deterrent. It discourages, and anyone can still press Enter.

stem: A self-storage business wants controls that discourage break-ins without blocking or recording anything.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.t: Signs warning that the site is monitored
options.why: Warning signs discourage an attempt without stopping it.

options.t: Bright lights over the storage rows
options.why: Bright lighting makes thieves feel seen, which discourages them.
Padlocks block entry, which is preventive.

options.t: An alarm log reviewed each morning
options.why: Reviewing an alarm log identifies events, which is detective.

options.t: Replacing broken locks after a theft
options.why: Repairing after a theft is corrective.

detail: without blocking or recording anything
explain: Warning signs and lighting are deterrent: they discourage without stopping. Padlocks block, log reviews detect and replacing locks corrects.

ask: Which of the following describes a detective control?

options.t: It blocks an event before it starts
options.why: That describes a preventive control.
That describes a deterrent control.

options.t: It identifies and records an event
options.why: Detective controls identify and record events so they can be investigated, without stopping them.

options.t: It repairs damage after an event
options.why: That describes a corrective control.

explain: A detective control identifies and records an event while it happens or after. It alerts but does not block.

ask: Which of the following controls is detective?

options.t: A firewall rule that drops inbound traffic
options.why: Dropping traffic blocks it, which is preventive.

options.t: A motion sensor that trips an alarm
options.why: The sensor identifies movement and raises an alarm.

options.t: A banner warning that misuse is prosecuted
options.why: A warning banner discourages, which is deterrent.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

explain: Log reviews, intrusion detection alerts and motion sensors are detective controls: they identify events rather than stopping them.

stem: A retailer's intrusion detection system raises an alert when it sees a known attack pattern on the store network, but the traffic still reaches its target.
ask: Which of the following control types does this system provide?

options.why: The system identifies the attack and alerts without blocking it.
The traffic still reaches its target, so nothing was blocked.
Nothing here discourages the attacker.
Nothing is repaired; an alert is raised.

detail: the traffic still reaches its target
explain: An intrusion detection system identifies and alerts but does not block, so it is detective. A prevention system that drops traffic would be preventive.

stem: A museum's motion sensors sound an alarm at the security desk when someone moves through a closed gallery after hours.
ask: Which of the following control types do the motion sensors provide?

options.why: The sensors lock nothing; the person can still move through the gallery.
The sensors work whether or not anyone knows of them; their job is to report movement.
Nothing is repaired; an alarm is raised.
The sensors identify movement and raise an alarm.

detail: sound an alarm at the security desk
explain: A motion sensor tripping an alarm is a standard detective control. It identifies the event so people can respond.

stem: A clinic's camera is hidden above a ceiling tile in the drug store room. Each morning a manager reviews its footage to see who entered overnight.
ask: Which of the following control types does the hidden camera serve?

options.why: A hidden camera cannot discourage anyone who does not know it is there.
The camera does not stop anyone entering.
The footage is reviewed to identify who entered, which is detective.
Reviewing footage repairs nothing.

detail: hidden above a ceiling tile
explain: Cameras whose footage is reviewed are detective. Because this one is hidden, it cannot also be deterrent.

stem: A hospital connects a sensor to a copy of its network traffic. The sensor alerts the security team when it sees an attack pattern, but it has no way to drop traffic.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sensor provide?

options.why: It cannot drop traffic, so it blocks nothing.
An alert repairs nothing.
The sensor identifies attacks and alerts, which is detective.
The sensor is not described as a substitute for a missing control.

detail: it has no way to drop traffic
explain: IDS (intrusion detection system) is detective and IPS (intrusion prevention system) is preventive. A sensor that can only alert is an IDS.

stem: A shipping firm's endpoint tool reports that a laptop is infected with malware. The removal is scheduled for the next morning.
ask: Which of the following control types did the endpoint tool's report provide?

options.why: Removing the malware tomorrow is corrective; the report only identified it.
The malware is already on the laptop, so nothing was blocked.
The report does not stand in for a missing control.
The report identified the infection, which is detective.

detail: The removal is scheduled for the next morning
explain: Detective is not corrective: discovering malware is detective, and removing it is corrective.

stem: An energy company's monitoring tool keeps a fingerprint of each configuration file on its control servers and sends an alert when a fingerprint changes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the monitoring tool provide?

options.why: The tool does not stop the file being changed.
The tool identifies a changed file and alerts after the change.
The tool does not tell anyone what to do; it reports a change.
The tool restores nothing; it alerts.

detail: sends an alert when a fingerprint changes
explain: File integrity monitoring is detective: the change has already happened, and the tool records and reports it.

stem: An analyst at a property management company reads the entries below.
ask: Which of the following control types does the last entry show at work?

lines: 08:41:02 sshd: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:09 sshd: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:19 sshd: Accepted password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:20 monitor: rule 'failures then success' fired, ticket 5521 opened

options.why: The rule identified the pattern and opened a ticket after it happened.
The login was accepted, so nothing was blocked.
Opening a ticket repairs nothing; locking the account afterward would be corrective.
No warning was shown to the attacker; the rule fired after the fact.

detail: rule 'failures then success' fired, ticket 5521 opened
explain: An alert rule that spots failed logins followed by a success is a detective control at work. Locking the account afterward would be the corrective step.

stem: An insurer's audit finds no way to learn that a break-in at its records room has happened. The audit asks for controls that identify and record such events.
ask: Which of the following meet the audit's request? (Select TWO)

options.t: A stronger lock on the door
options.why: A lock blocks entry, which is preventive, and records nothing.

options.t: A sign warning that intruders are prosecuted
options.why: A warning sign discourages, which is deterrent.

options.t: A motion sensor wired to the alarm panel
options.why: The sensor identifies movement in the room and raises an alarm.

options.t: A door access log reviewed every morning
options.why: A reviewed access log records entries and lets people spot a break-in.

options.t: A procedure for replacing stolen files
options.why: Replacing what was taken is corrective, after the event.

detail: controls that identify and record such events
explain: Motion sensors and reviewed access logs are detective controls. Locks prevent, signs deter and recovery procedures correct.

ask: Which of the following describes a corrective control?

options.t: It restores operations after an event
options.why: Corrective controls act after an event to limit damage and return to normal.

options.t: It substitutes for a safeguard that cannot be used
options.why: That describes a compensating control.

options.t: It blocks an event before it happens
options.why: That describes a preventive control.

options.t: It tells people what they must do
options.why: That describes a directive control.

explain: A corrective control is applied after an event to limit damage and restore systems. Compensating, in contrast, substitutes for a control that cannot be used.

ask: Which of the following controls is corrective?

options.t: An isolated network for an old system
options.why: Isolating a system that cannot take the ideal control is compensating.
A sign that instructs is directive.
Restoring data after an event returns operations to normal.
Reviewing logs identifies events, which is detective.

explain: Backups and restoration are the classic corrective controls. They act after the event.

stem: Malware wiped the order database at a bicycle wholesaler on Tuesday. On Wednesday the database administrator loaded Monday's copy, and the company resumed taking orders.
ask: Which of the following control types does loading Monday's copy provide?

options.why: Nothing stands in for a missing control; the damage is being repaired.
Loading the saved copy repairs the damage after the event and restores operations.
Finding the damage would be detective; loading the copy repairs it.
The attack already happened, so nothing is being blocked.

detail: Malware wiped the order database
explain: Restoring data from a backup after an attack is corrective. It limits damage and returns the business to normal.

stem: After an attacker used a flaw in a hotel's booking site, the response team removed the attacker's files and installed the vendor's fix for the flaw.
ask: Which of the following control types do the response team's actions provide?

options.why: The flaw was already exploited, so the fix repairs rather than blocks an attack that already happened.
The team applied the real fix, not a substitute for a control that cannot be used.
The actions remove and fix; they do not identify the event.
Removing the attacker's files and patching the hole after the attack is corrective.

detail: After an attacker used a flaw
explain: An incident response process that removes malicious files and patches the hole is corrective: it acts after the event.

stem: A university help desk learns that a professor's password was posted on a public forum and resets the password at once.
ask: Which of the following control types does the reset provide?

options.why: The exposure already happened; the reset repairs its effect.
Learning about the post is detective; the reset is the repair.
The reset does not tell anyone what to do.
The password was already exposed; resetting it limits the damage after the event.

detail: was posted on a public forum
explain: Resetting a compromised password is corrective: it acts after the event to restore a secure state.

stem: Malware spread from an old controller at a packaging factory. The team cleaned the controller and, because it cannot run security software, moved it to an isolated network segment.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes cleaning the controller?

options.why: The move to an isolated segment is compensating, but the stem asks about cleaning the controller.
Cleaning the controller repairs damage after the event.
Cleaning does not identify the event; it repairs it.
Cleaning does not instruct anyone.

detail: The team cleaned the controller
edge: The isolation stands in for security software the controller cannot run, which is compensating, but the cleaning repairs damage after the event, which is corrective.
explain: The stem holds two controls. Cleaning after the outbreak is corrective; the isolation that stands in for missing security software is compensating.

stem: A scan at a school finds a remote access trojan on a teacher's laptop. The IT staff then wipe the laptop and reinstall it from a clean image.
ask: Which of the following control types does the reinstall provide?

options.why: Wiping and reinstalling removes the infection and returns the laptop to a clean state.
The scan that found the trojan is detective; the reinstall repairs.
The laptop was already infected, so nothing is being blocked.
Nothing stands in for a missing control.

detail: wipe the laptop and reinstall it from a clean image
explain: Reimaging an infected machine is corrective. The scan that found the infection was the detective control.

stem: A web host learns that an intruder copied the private key for one of its certificates, and it revokes that certificate the same day.
ask: Which of the following control types does revoking the certificate provide?

options.why: The theft already happened; revoking repairs its effect rather than blocking it.
Learning of the theft is detective; revoking is the repair.
The key was already stolen; revoking the certificate limits the damage after the event.
Revoking does not discourage anyone; it cancels the stolen certificate.

detail: an intruder copied the private key
explain: Revoking a stolen certificate is a corrective control: it acts after the event to limit damage.

stem: The incident record below comes from a car rental company.
ask: Which of the following control types does the 11:45 entry record?

lines: 09:12  INC-3307 opened: ransom note found on shared drive S
09:30  Shared drive S taken offline
11:45  Shared drive S restored from the 02:00 snapshot, users reconnected

options.why: The ransom note being found at 09:12 is detection; 11:45 restores service.
Restoring the drive from a snapshot returns operations to normal after the event.
The attack already happened; nothing is being blocked.
Nothing stands in for a missing control.

detail: restored from the 02:00 snapshot, users reconnected
explain: Restoring data after ransomware is corrective. The 09:12 discovery was the detective step.

stem: A clothing store's checkout server was infected with malware last night. The manager asks for the controls that limit the damage now and bring the server back.
ask: Which of the following meet the request? (Select TWO)

options.t: Removing the malware from the server
options.why: Removing the infection after the event limits the damage.

options.t: A login banner warning against misuse
options.why: A warning banner discourages future misuse; it repairs nothing.

options.t: Restoring the server from a clean backup
options.why: Restoring returns the server to normal operation after the event.

options.t: A policy banning personal USB drives
options.why: A policy tells people what to do in the future; it repairs nothing now.

options.t: An alert rule for future infections
options.why: An alert identifies a future event; it does not bring the server back.

detail: limit the damage now and bring the server back
explain: Corrective controls act after the event: removing malware and restoring from backup. The others deter, direct or detect.

ask: Which of the following describes a compensating control?

options.t: A stand-in for a measure that cannot be used
options.why: A compensating control gives similar protection when the required control cannot be put in place.

options.t: A repair made after an incident has happened
options.why: That describes a corrective control.

options.t: A barrier that stops an event before it starts
options.why: That describes a preventive control.

options.t: An instruction telling people what to do
options.why: That describes a directive control.

explain: A compensating control is an alternative used when the primary or required control cannot be implemented. It is not the same as corrective.

ask: Which of the following situations calls for a compensating control?

options.t: An attack has already caused damage
options.why: Repairing damage after an attack calls for a corrective control.

options.t: An attacker should be discouraged from trying
options.why: Discouraging attempts calls for a deterrent control.

options.t: An event must be spotted as it happens
options.why: Spotting events calls for a detective control.

options.t: A required safeguard cannot be put in place
options.why: Compensating controls exist for exactly this case.

explain: Compensating controls come up when a system cannot take the ideal control, such as legacy equipment. They substitute for it, often for a while.

stem: A city's traffic signal controller runs firmware that cannot accept security updates. Until the controller is replaced, the city places it behind a firewall that admits connections from just two engineering laptops.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the firewall arrangement?

options.why: The firewall does block traffic, but it is there because the updates cannot be applied.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The firewall stands in for the security updates the controller cannot accept.
The firewall enforces access; it does not just tell people what to do.

detail: cannot accept security updates
edge: The firewall blocks traffic like any preventive control, but it was added because the required updates cannot be applied, which makes it a compensating control.
explain: Placing equipment that cannot be patched behind strict network rules until it is replaced is the textbook compensating control.

stem: A two-person accounting office cannot split payment duties between different people. To make up for this, the owner reviews every payment record at the end of each day.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the owner's daily review?

options.why: Reviewing records is detective work, but it is done because the duties cannot be split.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The review stands in for the separation of duties the office cannot have.
The review does not tell anyone what to do.

detail: cannot split payment duties between different people
edge: Reviewing records is detective in method, but the stem says it is there to make up for duties that cannot be split, which makes it compensating.
explain: Extra review where separation of duties is impossible is a compensating control. A control standing in for one that cannot be used is compensating first.

stem: A factory's milling machine runs software that cannot run antivirus. Until the machine is replaced, the plant keeps it off the network and loads files onto it only from one checked USB drive.
ask: Which of the following control types does the plant's arrangement provide?

options.why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The arrangement is enforced, not just an instruction to staff.
Nothing here aims to discourage an attacker.
Keeping the machine off the network stands in for the antivirus it cannot run.

detail: cannot run antivirus
explain: When legacy equipment cannot take the ideal control, isolating it until it is replaced is a compensating control.

stem: A water utility's standard requires multifactor sign-in, but its old billing application cannot support it. Users now reach the application only through a gateway server that does require multifactor sign-in.
ask: Which of the following describes the role the gateway plays here?

options.t: It repairs the software after a breach
options.why: Nothing was breached; repairing after an event would be corrective.

options.t: It stands in for a feature the app lacks
options.why: The gateway gives the multifactor protection the application itself cannot provide, which is compensating.

options.t: It records each sign-in for later review
options.why: The gateway enforces a second factor; it does not only record sign-ins.

options.t: It tells staff how to sign in safely
options.why: Users are not just told what to do; the gateway enforces the second factor.

detail: its old billing application cannot support it
explain: A gateway that enforces multifactor sign-in for a system that cannot support it addresses the same risk by other means, which is compensating.

stem: A retailer's standard requires an endpoint agent on every computer, but the agent cannot run on three old kiosks. The security team writes an approved exception, adds strict network rules for the kiosks and sets a review date.
ask: Which of the following control types do the strict network rules provide in this case?

options.why: The rules stand in for the agent the kiosks cannot run.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The rules are enforced by the network, not instructions to staff.
The rules do not aim to discourage anyone.

detail: the agent cannot run on three old kiosks
explain: A compensating control is documented as an exception, approved and reviewed until the original control is possible. Here the network rules stand in for the agent.

stem: A small clinic's insurer recommends a night guard for the records room, which the clinic cannot provide. With the insurer's approval, the clinic installs a monitored alarm on the room's door instead.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the alarm in this case?

options.why: The alarm is an approved substitute for the guard the clinic cannot provide.
The alarm detects entry, but it was put in place instead of a recommended guard.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The alarm does not tell anyone what to do.
